explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. God says, “…the land itself must observe a Sabbath to the LORD.” (Leviticus 25:2) Not just the people. The dirt gets a day off too, and I know folks who can't rest half as well as a field can.
I get the thinking, since a house is a nice place to put your feet up. But the verse says the land itself must observe the Sabbath. Houses show up later in the chapter, and they get their own rules.

A resting shovel sounds lovely, and I bet my stamper handle would sign up fast. But God doesn't say the tools. He says the land itself must observe a Sabbath to Him. The tools sit idle because the field is resting.

Not this time, friend. God says, “You are not to reap the aftergrowth of your harvest or gather the grapes of your untended vines.” That's the Sabbath year. The land must have a year of complete rest.

Right. In the Sabbath year, God says, “You are not to reap the aftergrowth of your harvest or gather the grapes of your untended vines.” The land must have a year of complete rest. So the vines get left alone, and that's the whole point.

explanations.answer: The household and even the wild animals
explanations.explanation: Yes! The food is for you, your manservant and maidservant, the hired hand or foreigner who stays with you, your livestock and the wild animals in your land. That's a wide table. Even the critters get a seat, and they didn't have to bring a dish.

explanations.answer: The widows and orphans of the town
explanations.explanation: Good heart on that guess, but these verses don't name widows or orphans. They list your household, the hired hand or foreigner staying with you, your livestock and the wild animals. Then verse 7 says, “All its growth may serve as food.”

These verses don't list priests or Levites here. Instead they name the household, the hired hand or foreigner who stays with you, the livestock and the wild animals. That's a surprisingly long guest list for a year with no sowing.

Yes, baker. God says to sound the horn far and wide “on the tenth day of the seventh month, the Day of Atonement.” You shall sound it throughout your land. That's a big day on the calendar, and the whole land hears it.
Passover is a big day, but it isn't the one named here. God says the horn sounds on the tenth day of the seventh month, the Day of Atonement. The horn goes out far and wide on that day.
That's a fair guess, but this verse names a different day. The horn sounds on the tenth day of the seventh month, the Day of Atonement. God says to sound it throughout the land.

explanations.answer: Back to his own property and clan
explanations.explanation: That's right. God says, “…each of you is to return to his property and to his clan.” Then verse 13 says it again, that each shall return to his own property. Liberty means going home.

explanations.answer: Up to the place God will choose
explanations.explanation: This passage doesn't say anything like that for the Jubilee. God says each person is to return to his property and to his clan. The direction is home, not up.

explanations.answer: Out to the fields to glean
explanations.explanation: The fields do matter in the Jubilee, since God says not to sow or reap. But the instruction for liberty is that each of you is to return to his property and to his clan. It's a homecoming year.

Yes! God says, “The fiftieth year will be a Jubilee for you; you are not to sow the land or reap its aftergrowth or harvest the untended vines.” (Leviticus 25:11) So the land rests in the seventh year and rests again in the fiftieth. Plenty of time to put its feet up.

It's true, friend, and it's an easy one to second-guess. God says, “The fiftieth year will be a Jubilee for you; you are not to sow the land or reap its aftergrowth or harvest the untended vines.” (Leviticus 25:11) The land rests then too, even though it already rests every seventh year.
Yes. More years before the Jubilee means more harvests to sell, so God says you “shall increase the price in proportion to a greater number of years.” It's all about the harvests the buyer will get.
Right. Fewer years left means fewer harvests, so God says to “decrease it in proportion to a lesser number of years.” Then He gives the reason: “…for he is selling you a given number of harvests.”
A fixed price would be easy, but the price moves with the years. God says to increase it for a greater number of years and decrease it for a lesser number. The count changes the price.
Nothing here is left to luck. God says to buy “according to the number of years since the last Jubilee,” and the seller sells according to the harvest years remaining. The price follows the count.

Nobody's hiding the price, baker. Both sides count the years since the last Jubilee and the harvest years remaining, and the price follows. God also says, “Do not take advantage of each other…” (Leviticus 25:17).

explanations.answer: They will dwell securely in the land
explanations.explanation: That's it. God says to keep His statutes and carefully observe His judgments “so that you may dwell securely in the land.” Verse 19 adds that they can eat their fill and dwell in safety.

explanations.answer: They will rule over the nations nearby
explanations.explanation: Ruling the neighbors is a big promise, but it isn't what God says here. He says keeping His statutes and judgments means they “may dwell securely in the land.” Security is the promise.

explanations.answer: Their enemies will make peace with them
explanations.explanation: These verses don't mention enemies at all. God says keeping His statutes and judgments is “so that you may dwell securely in the land.” Then the land yields its fruit and they dwell in safety.

explanations.answer: Yields a crop for three years
explanations.explanation: Yes! God says, “But I will send My blessing upon you in the sixth year, so that the land will yield a crop sufficient for three years.” That answers the worry about what they'd eat in the seventh year. God answers their question before they even have to ask it twice.

explanations.answer: Yields only enough for one year
explanations.explanation: One year's worth wouldn't carry them through a year of rest, and that isn't what God says. He says the land will yield “a crop sufficient for three years.” That's His blessing in the sixth year.
The verse doesn't split it up like that. God says His blessing in the sixth year means the land will yield “a crop sufficient for three years.” It's one blessing, and it's big.

explanations.answer: Because the land belongs to the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the heart of it. God says, “The land must not be sold permanently, because it is Mine, and you are but foreigners and residents with Me.” It's His land, so nobody sells it for good.

explanations.answer: Because the land belongs to the priests
explanations.explanation: The priests aren't named as owners here. God says the land can't be sold permanently “because it is Mine.” He's the owner, and the Israelites are foreigners and residents with Him.

explanations.answer: Because the land belongs to the king
explanations.explanation: No king is mentioned in this passage. God says the land can't be sold permanently “because it is Mine.” The deed is His, and everybody else is a resident.
Right. God says, “…his nearest of kin may come and redeem what his brother has sold.” Family steps in. It's a good thing to have someone like that in your corner.
The high priest isn't named in these verses. God says it's the man's nearest of kin who may come and redeem what his brother sold. The job stays in the family.
The elders aren't mentioned here. The verse says his nearest of kin may come and redeem what was sold. It's a family matter.
Yes. God says, “he shall calculate the years since its sale, repay the balance to the man to whom he sold it, and return to his property.” It's a count of years, and then home he goes.
Tithes don't come up in this part of the chapter. The man calculates the years since the sale, repays the balance to the buyer, and returns to his property. The count is years.
Feasts would make for a fun calculation, but that isn't what God says. The man calculates the years since the sale and repays the balance. Then he returns to his property.

Not quite, friend. God says that if he can't obtain enough to repay, what he sold stays with the buyer “until the Year of Jubilee.” Then it says, “In the Jubilee, however, it is to be released, so that he may return to his property.” It doesn't stay forever.

That's right. If he can't get enough to repay, the land stays with the buyer only until the Year of Jubilee. Then God says, “In the Jubilee, however, it is to be released, so that he may return to his property.”

explanations.answer: Help him so he can keep living among them
explanations.explanation: Yes. God says to help him “as you would a foreigner or stranger, so that he can continue to live among you.” The goal is for him to stay in the community.

explanations.answer: Send him to the priests to be cared for
explanations.explanation: Priests aren't mentioned in this verse. God tells the people, “you are to help him,” so that he can continue to live among you. The help comes from the neighbors.

explanations.answer: Leave his own clan to deal with him
explanations.explanation: That's not what God says. He says, “you are to help him as you would a foreigner or stranger, so that he can continue to live among you.” The instruction is to help.

That's right. God says, “Do not take any interest or profit from him, but fear your God, that your countryman may live among you.” No interest, no profit. The goal is that he can keep living among them.
A cloak isn't mentioned in this passage. What God says not to take is “any interest or profit.” That's the instruction for helping a destitute countryman.
A tenth isn't mentioned in this passage. God says, “Do not take any interest or profit from him.” Then He reminds them to fear their God.

explanations.answer: As a hired worker and not a slave
explanations.explanation: Yes. God says, “you must not force him into slave labor.” Instead he stays “as a hired worker or temporary resident” until the Year of Jubilee.

explanations.answer: As a slave for the rest of his life
explanations.explanation: That isn't what God says for a countryman. He says, “you must not force him into slave labor,” and the man works only until the Year of Jubilee. Verse 46 says no man may rule harshly over his brother, the Israelites.

explanations.answer: As a prisoner until he pays up
explanations.explanation: A prisoner isn't in the picture. God says the man stays as a hired worker or temporary resident, and he works until the Year of Jubilee.
Yes! God says, “Then he and his children are to be released, and he may return to his clan and to the property of his fathers.” The Year of Jubilee frees him, children and all. Everybody goes home.

It's true, baker. In the Year of Jubilee, “he and his children are to be released, and he may return to his clan and to the property of his fathers.” (Leviticus 25:41) The Jubilee frees the whole family.

explanations.answer: They're His servants He brought out of Egypt
explanations.explanation: That's right. God says, “Because the Israelites are My servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt, they are not to be sold as slaves.” Their belonging starts with Him.

explanations.answer: There are too few of them to spare
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about their numbers. God's reason is, “the Israelites are My servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt.” That's why they are not to be sold as slaves.

explanations.answer: Their fathers made a vow at Sinai
explanations.explanation: A vow isn't mentioned in this passage. God gives His own reason: they are His servants, whom He brought out of the land of Egypt.

Not here, friend. God says, “…as for your brothers, the Israelites, no man may rule harshly over his brother.” (Leviticus 25:46) He says it again in verse 43: “You are not to rule over them harshly, but you shall fear your God.”

That's right. God says, “…as for your brothers, the Israelites, no man may rule harshly over his brother.” (Leviticus 25:46) He says the same in verse 43: “You are not to rule over them harshly, but you shall fear your God.”

Yes. The word in the text is redeem, and here it means one of his brothers pays the price to buy him back. God says that may be his uncle, his cousin or any close relative from his clan. Family can step in.
Being sent back is a nice thought, but the text says he can be redeemed. A price is figured in verses 50 to 52, so the word is bought back. His uncle, cousin or any close relative may do it.
Being called back sounds friendly, but the text says redeemed. A price is worked out based on the years left until the Jubilee. That means bought back.
Not quite. God says, “Even if he is not redeemed in any of these ways, he and his children shall be released in the Year of Jubilee.” (Leviticus 25:54) So the Jubilee frees him either way.
Right. Even if nobody buys him back, God says, “he and his children shall be released in the Year of Jubilee.” (Leviticus 25:54) The Jubilee frees him, and his children go free with him.
